triage.reason: Classic sore throat presentation where history, exam and rapid strep or culture lead to diagnosis and management decisions including when to treat or refer.

demographics: Most common in children over age 2; nearly every child in the US has at least one episode
Bacterial (strep) tonsillitis peaks in children ages 5–15
Viral tonsillitis is more common in younger children
Adults can get it but it is much less common

risk_factors.text: Close contact with someone who has a sore throat or strep throat
Crowded settings such as school or daycare

social_history: Household contacts with recent sore throat
exposures: Contact with a person who has strep throat or a viral upper respiratory infection

hpi.onset: Sudden or fairly rapid over a day or two
hpi.progression: Sore throat builds over 1–2 days, is worst for a few days, then gradually improves; fever often comes first in children
hpi.location: Throat, centered on the tonsils on both sides
hpi.quality: Scratchy and raw, then constant and painful, worse with swallowing
hpi.severity: Mild to severe; often 5–8/10 at its worst
hpi.timing: Constant, worse on waking and with swallowing

associated_symptoms.text: White or yellow patches on the tonsils
Nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain (more in children)
Cough or runny nose (suggests viral cause)
Hoarse voice or changes in voice

pertinent_negatives: One-sided severe throat pain with uvula deviation
Cough as the main symptom (points to viral or other cause)

positives.text: White or yellow coating on the tonsils

negatives: One-sided throat swelling with uvula deviation
argues_against: Drooling or trouble breathing (suggests epiglottitis or deep neck infection)
One-sided severe pain with uvula deviation (suggests peritonsillar abscess)
Cough and runny nose as the main symptoms (more typical of viral URI)
Profuse diarrhea or vomiting before the sore throat
Diffuse rash with peeling (suggests other conditions such as Kawasaki disease)
Stiff neck or confusion (suggests meningitis or other serious infection)

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children may not complain of sore throat; they present with fever, irritability, poor feeding, vomiting or abdominal pain.
Less common and often milder; fever may be low-grade or absent and throat pain less prominent.
Can be more severe, with higher fever, more extensive swelling and slower resolution; may need broader evaluation.

general.mild: Alert, comfortable, speaking normally, no respiratory distress
general.moderate: Uncomfortable, prefers not to talk, mild fever flush, no distress at rest
general.severe: Ill-appearing, febrile, drooling or refusing to swallow, sitting upright
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, tripod posture, stridor or respiratory distress, unable to swallow secretions

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oropharynx with a tongue blade and good light
Inspect the tonsillar surface for exudate
findings.finding: White or yellow patches or coating on the tonsils
Diffuse erythema of the pharyngeal mucosa

findings.maneuver: Palpate the anterior cervical chain bilaterally
findings.finding: Tender, enlarged anterior cervical lymph nodes

findings.maneuver: Note breath odor during the oropharyngeal exam
Inspect the position of the uvula at rest
findings.finding: Uvula deviated away from one tonsil with asymmetric swelling

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to open the mouth fully
Listen to the patient's voice during history
Auscultate over the neck and chest while the patient breathes quietly
Observe the patient's ability to handle oral secretions
Flex the neck passively and assess for resistance

findings.finding: Clear breath sounds without crackles or wheezing

labs.caveat: Leukocytosis is more typical of bacterial (strep) tonsillitis; viral tonsillitis usually has a normal or mildly low white count. A normal count does not exclude strep.
Neutrophilic predominance favors a bacterial cause; lymphocytosis favors viral.
Relative lymphocytosis supports a viral cause.
Nonspecific; may be mildly elevated in both viral and bacterial tonsillitis and does not distinguish them.
Nonspecific inflammatory marker; not needed for routine diagnosis.
Not part of routine tonsillitis workup; may be mildly elevated in bacterial infection.

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected epiglottitis or airway obstruction when the diagnosis is unclear
Suspected peritonsillar abscess or deep neck space infection

findings.text: Peritonsillar fluid collection with rim enhancement
Asymmetric tonsillar enlargement and surrounding fat stranding
Extension into parapharyngeal or retropharyngeal space

imaging.study: Ultrasound of the neck (transcutaneous or intraoral)
imaging.preferred_when: Children or pregnancy when peritonsillar abscess is suspected and CT is not desired

initial.why: Fast, in-office test for group A streptococcal pharyngitis; positive result confirms bacterial cause and guides antibiotic treatment
More reliable than rapid test; used to confirm strep when rapid test is negative, especially in children and adolescents
initial.only_if: rapid strep test is negative and bacterial cause is still suspected

initial.why: May show leukocytosis with left shift in bacterial tonsillitis; not routinely required
initial.only_if: systemic illness, severe symptoms, or diagnostic uncertainty

supporting.why: Nonspecific marker of inflammation; may support bacterial cause but does not distinguish viral from bacterial
Nonspecific inflammatory marker; rarely changes management
Evaluates for peritonsillar abscess or deep neck space infection
supporting.only_if: severe unilateral pain, trismus, muffled voice, uvular deviation, or drooling

supporting.test: Ultrasound of the neck (transcutaneous or intraoral)
supporting.why: Alternative to CT for suspected peritonsillar abscess, especially in children or pregnancy
supporting.only_if: peritonsillar abscess suspected and CT is contraindicated or not preferred

not_indicated.why: No established role in upper respiratory tract infections like tonsillitis
Not useful for tonsillitis; may be ordered only when epiglottitis is suspected
not_indicated.only_if: epiglottitis or airway obstruction is suspected

decision_points: Use rapid strep test first; if negative in a child or adolescent, confirm with throat culture before withholding antibiotics
Do not treat viral tonsillitis with antibiotics; supportive care only
Consider peritonsillar abscess or epiglottitis if there is drooling, trismus, muffled voice, uvular deviation, or respiratory distress; obtain urgent imaging or specialist evaluation
Recurrent tonsillitis or obstructive symptoms may warrant referral for tonsillectomy

criteria.name: Centor criteria (modified McIsaac)
criteria.summary: Clinical prediction of group A streptococcal pharyngitis using tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes, fever, absence of cough, and age. Helps decide whether to test or treat empirically.
items: Age (3–14 years, 15–44 years, or 45 years and older)

differential.name: Peritonsillar abscess
differential.why_considered: Severe sore throat with tonsillar swelling and fever; a common complication of tonsillitis that can mimic it
differential.trigger: Unilateral severe throat pain with trismus, muffled voice, drooling, or uvular deviation

history: Pain is one-sided and worsening despite antibiotics
Drooling or unable to swallow saliva
exam: Uvula deviated away from the affected side
imaging: CT neck with contrast shows a rim-enhancing peritonsillar fluid collection
Intraoral or transcutaneous ultrasound shows a fluid collection

differential.name: Epiglottitis
differential.why_considered: Sore throat with fever and difficulty swallowing; a life-threatening airway emergency that can be mistaken for tonsillitis
differential.trigger: Drooling, stridor, tripod posture, or rapidly worsening difficulty breathing

labs: Blood cultures may grow the causative organism
imaging: Lateral neck x-ray shows a thumb sign (enlarged epiglottis)
Direct visualization shows a swollen, cherry-red epiglottis

differential.name: Infectious mononucleosis
differential.why_considered: Sore throat with fever, tonsillar exudate and swollen neck glands; often mistaken for strep tonsillitis

history: Prolonged fatigue and malaise for days to weeks
Sore throat that persists despite antibiotics
Close contact with a person who has mononucleosis
labs: Positive heterophile antibody (Monospot) or EBV-specific antibodies

differential.name: Viral pharyngitis
differential.why_considered: Sore throat with red tonsils and fever; the most common cause of tonsillitis and clinically similar

history: Cough, runny nose, or hoarseness as prominent symptoms
exam: Diffuse pharyngeal erythema without tonsillar exudate
Conjunctivitis or oral ulcers (suggesting viral cause)
labs: Negative rapid strep test and throat culture
Normal or mildly low white count

differential.name: Scarlet fever
differential.why_considered: Tonsillitis caused by group A strep with a characteristic rash; a bacterial complication that requires treatment

history: Sore throat followed by a rash
exam: Sandpaper-like rash on the trunk and extremities
labs: Positive rapid strep test or throat culture

differential.name: Diphtheria
differential.why_considered: Severe sore throat with a thick tonsillar membrane; rare in the US but must be recognized

exam: Grayish adherent pseudomembrane on tonsils that bleeds when removed
labs: Culture on tellurite or Loeffler medium

differential.name: Kawasaki disease
differential.why_considered: Fever and sore throat in a young child; can present with red throat and tonsillar swelling

exam: Red cracked lips and strawberry tongue
Rash, extremity changes, and cervical lymphadenopathy
imaging: Echocardiogram may show coronary artery dilation

severity.mild: Sore throat with mild pain, low-grade or no fever, able to eat and drink, no respiratory symptoms
severity.moderate: Moderate to severe pain, fever, difficulty swallowing, enlarged tender cervical nodes, but no airway compromise
severity.severe: Severe pain, high fever, drooling or inability to swallow, trismus, muffled voice, or signs of dehydration
severity.critical: Airway obstruction or deep neck infection with stridor, respiratory distress, or sepsis

red_flags.finding: Drooling or inability to swallow saliva
red_flags.meaning: Suggests epiglottitis or peritonsillar abscess with airway compromise; needs urgent evaluation
Suggests peritonsillar abscess or deep neck infection
Possible sepsis or deep neck infection

red_flags.finding: Unilateral severe pain with neck swelling

special_populations.differences: Young children may not complain of sore throat; they present with fever, irritability, poor feeding, vomiting, or abdominal pain. Bacterial tonsillitis is most common in ages 5–15.
Less common and often milder; fever may be low-grade or absent and throat pain less prominent. Higher risk of complications if immunocompromised.
Can be more severe with higher fever, more extensive swelling, and slower resolution; may require broader evaluation and treatment.
Diagnosis and treatment are similar, but antibiotic choices should be reviewed for safety in pregnancy.

key_questions.question: When did the sore throat start, and how has it changed since then?
key_questions.looking_for: Sudden onset over 1–2 days with sore throat as the main complaint; gradual onset with prominent cough and runny nose favors a viral cause

key_questions.question: Does it hurt when you swallow? How bad is it?
key_questions.looking_for: Painful swallowing is typical; inability to swallow saliva or drooling suggests a deep neck infection or epiglottitis

key_questions.question: Is the pain on both sides or just one side?
key_questions.looking_for: Bilateral pain fits tonsillitis; severe one-sided pain suggests peritonsillar abscess

key_questions.question: Have you had a fever or chills?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever supports infection; high fever with systemic illness raises concern for a bacterial cause or complication

key_questions.question: Do you have a cough or runny nose?
key_questions.looking_for: Prominent cough and rhinorrhea point to a viral cause; absence of cough favors group A strep

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any white patches on your tonsils or bad breath?
key_questions.looking_for: Tonsillar exudate and halitosis support tonsillitis and are part of the Centor criteria

key_questions.question: Have you had any trouble breathing, drooling, or a muffled voice?
key_questions.looking_for: Any of these suggests airway compromise, epiglottitis, or peritonsillar abscess and requires urgent evaluation

key_questions.question: Can you open your mouth fully? Does it feel stiff?
key_questions.looking_for: Trismus suggests peritonsillar abscess or deep neck infection

key_questions.question: Has anyone around you had a sore throat or strep throat recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Close contact with strep supports a bacterial cause; sick contacts with cold symptoms support viral

key_questions.question: Have you had this before? How often?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent tonsillitis may prompt referral for tonsillectomy

key_questions.question: Are you taking any antibiotics or pain medicine for this?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent antibiotics may mask or modify the presentation; acetaminophen or ibuprofen use guides dosing advice

key_questions.question: Do you have any medication allergies, especially to penicillin?
key_questions.looking_for: Penicillin allergy changes the antibiotic choice if strep is confirmed

reasoning_points: Sore throat with painful swallowing, fever, and red swollen tonsils
Tonsillar exudate and tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy on exam
Absence of cough and runny nose favors a bacterial (group A strep) cause
Rapid strep test or throat culture confirms or excludes group A streptococcal infection
No drooling, stridor, trismus, muffled voice, or uvular deviation to suggest a deep neck infection or airway emergency
Viral causes are managed with supportive care; bacterial causes require antibiotics

easy: Child or adolescent with sudden sore throat, fever, and painful swallowing
Red swollen tonsils with white exudate and tender neck glands
medium: Viral tonsillitis with cough and runny nose and a negative rapid strep test
Adolescent with prolonged fatigue and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy suggesting mononucleosis
Young child with fever, vomiting, and abdominal pain but no clear complaint of sore throat
Scarlet fever with rash and strawberry tongue
hard: Severe one-sided throat pain with trismus and muffled voice suggesting peritonsillar abscess
Drooling or stridor suggesting epiglottitis or airway compromise
Immunocompromised patient with severe, slowly resolving tonsillitis
Older adult with mild sore throat and low-grade fever where the diagnosis is less obvious
